meta.body:
## Overview

Builds on #65282: the first commit here is #65282's, and this PR's change is the second. With priority scheduling, a high-priority request's first tokens share every step with lower-priority prefill chunks, which make those steps long. This PR adds `--priority-prefill-budget-cap` (off by default): until a higher-priority request has its first `--priority-prefill-budget-cap-tokens` output tokens (16 by default), lower-priority prefills are held back.

## Claims

- With the cap on, prefills of a strictly lower priority, running or waiting, sit out the steps in which a higher-priority request awaits its first `--priority-prefill-budget-cap-tokens` output tokens, with or without async scheduling: from the step in which it fits (a free running slot and KV cache room for its whole sequence) or, with a running slot free, its KV connector load is done.
- A request scheduled nothing, running or waiting, its KV load done or not, or a KV load still in flight, holds prefill back for at most that many steps in a row, and a lower-priority request that holds KV blocks sits out only while a request of its priority or a lower one runs, which preemption takes first.
- Decodes are never held, nor is a request with one token left to compute, nor a prefill midway through an encoder input while a request it is held for needs encoder cache space.
- Off by default, and off it changes no schedule: 2,496 traced configurations schedule as #65282 does, step for step.
- Counters, `vllm:priority_prefill_held_steps` and `vllm:priority_prefill_held_tokens`, registered only with the cap on.
- On an RTX 5060 Ti, behind three lower-priority prefills, a priority 0 chat turn's 16th token comes after 560 ms instead of 1,374 ms on v0.32.0 (1,242 ms with #65282 alone).

## Validation

**Tests** on CPU, as in #65282:

| Tests | main | this PR |
|---|---:|---:|
| `tests/v1/core/test_priority_make_room.py` (new, both PRs' tests) | — | 109 passed |
| the new file and five scheduler test files | 353 passed | 462 passed |
| the rest of `tests/v1/core`, `tests/engine/test_arg_utils.py`, `tests/v1/streaming_input` | 1,048 passed, 13 failed, 6 errors | the same |

The failures and errors are main's own, the same tests in both columns, with the one config check lifted as in #65282. Of 88 single-point mutants of the two changes before this rebase, all 80 that change a schedule fail a test. The other 8 change none: 7 only undo cost optimizations, and one drops the check that a KV load in flight is not done yet, which a done load makes redundant by holding prefill back on its own. Since #65285, main keeps a KV load in flight outside the in-flight prefills, except under HiSparse, so the hold now records each load's first step where the load is parked, in that order. Of the record's 8 single-point mutants, the 4 that change a schedule fail a test: dropping the record, or ending a load's hold a step early in either of two ways, fails 7 tests, and dropping it under HiSparse alone fails the test of the hold there. The other 4 change none: three only leave promoted, freed or expired loads in the record, which the holders' check skips, and one loosens that check where the record's order already ensures it.

**Liveness**, on the real scheduler on CPU: 400,000 random workloads on small KV pools, with KV loads, shared prefixes, streaming sessions, preemption and async scheduling, half of them also with failed loads, aborts, encoder inputs, prefill throttling and draft tokens, and 60,000 more with LoRA limits, connector lookups answered later, grammars, pause windows, sliding-window groups and `--disable-chunked-mm-input`, each run with the options off and on. A stall the options cause, one that resumes when both are turned off at the stalled step, occurs in 241 of the 400,000 and 100 of the 60,000 on earlier revisions, and in none now. The other stalls do not end with the options off, in states main reaches too: nothing is running and the request at the head of the waiting queues, usually `kv_holding_waiting`, cannot be admitted, such as a streaming session's next chunk that needs blocks held by two finished KV loads behind it; or, in 6 of the 60,000, a running request waits at an image longer than the long prefill threshold. 5,578 of the 400,000 end stuck with the options off, 5,287 with them on. On this rebase, each of the 400,000 ends as it did, seed by seed, and the 60,000 have the same stalls and totals. The search is in [Flatshare](https://github.com/StevenWang-CY/flatshare) (`benchmarks/results/2026-11-05-liveness/`).

**On a GPU**, in #65282's setup and session (vLLM v0.32.0 with both changes backported at their revision of 3 November, this PR's `5aae512d0`; this revision, backported too, schedules the case step for step as that one does, replayed on CPU; `N = 2`, the cap at 16 tokens): three priority 2 requests of 10,000 prompt tokens prefill when a priority 0 chat turn of about 750 tokens arrives (four runs):

| Scheduler | Priority 0 TTFT | Its 16th token |
|---|---:|---:|
| v0.32.0 | 420 ms (325–541) | 1,374 ms (1,236–1,514) |
| with #65282 | 328 ms (257–470) | 1,242 ms (1,164–1,429) |
| with #65282 and this change | 292 ms (232–325) | 560 ms (518–582) |

The turn's tokens come 60–66 ms apart on v0.32.0 and 17–20 ms apart with this change. End to end, in #65282's five rounds of two voice calls beside 24 coding-agent sessions (medians), the calls' voice-to-voice p95 falls from 5,085 ms with #65282 alone to 3,094 ms, or 2,232 ms with a 48-token window; on an A100 SXM4 80 GB, both changes with a 48-token window take it from 4,986 ms on v0.32.0 to 1,634 ms. The end-to-end runs are text only and used an earlier revision of the hold, which also held a request with one token left, kept the first held request's KV load from starting, and held for a waiting request or a finished KV load without a bound.

**CPU cost of `schedule()`**, in #65282's grid, before the rebases and the revision of 5 November, which adds a dictionary lookup and update for each holder: with the cap alone, a step costs up to 93 µs more, or 284 µs when the head has a 999-block prefix cache hit; with both options, a step that preempts costs 344 to 790 µs more. With both off, it costs what main's does (−34 to +24 µs of main over 17 states). The table was not measured again on `821851eab`. Since this rebase, the hold records each KV load's first step where the load is parked, rather than rebuilding the record from every load in flight each step: with 4,096 loads in flight past their first steps, finding the holders takes 0.6 µs a step instead of 0.70 ms, and a step with both options and every running slot taken costs 0.34 and 4.2 ms with 512 and 4,096 loads in flight, against 0.36 and 4.6 ms before, most of it #65282's scan for the request to make room for, measured as in #65282.

<details>
<summary>The 17 states, in µs</summary>

| A, 64 running, 100 waiting, a 999-block hit, 500 free | 517 | 576 (+59) | 546 (+29) | 511 (−6) |
| A, 64 running, 100 waiting, no hit | 223 | 237 (+15) | 245 (+22) | 227 (+4) |
| B, 16 running, 1,000 waiting | 102 | 208 (+106) | 156 (+54) | 106 (+3) |
| B, 64 running, 1,000 waiting | 264 | 360 (+96) | 301 (+37) | 258 (−6) |
| B, 256 running, 1,000 waiting | 863 | 1,034 (+172) | 886 (+23) | 862 (−1) |
| B, 256 running, 10 waiting | 828 | 1,020 (+191) | 921 (+93) | 834 (+6) |
| B, 64 running, 100 waiting, a 999-block hit, 500 free | 507 | 932 (+426) | 791 (+284) | 505 (−2) |
| C, 16 running, 1,000 waiting | 54 | 105 (+51) | 102 (+48) | 56 (+2) |
| C, 64 running, 1,000 waiting | 212 | 280 (+67) | 248 (+35) | 201 (−12) |
| C, 256 running, 1,000 waiting | 845 | 929 (+84) | 844 (−1) | 811 (−34) |
| F, 16 running, 1,000 waiting | 176 | 519 (+344) | 193 (+17) | 182 (+6) |
| F, 64 running, 1,000 waiting | 351 | 875 (+525) | 402 (+51) | 364 (+13) |
| F, 256 running, 1,000 waiting | 1,445 | 2,235 (+790) | 1,508 (+63) | 1,429 (−17) |
| F, 4 running, 100 waiting, 16,000-token prompts | 118 | 841 (+723) | 141 (+23) | 124 (+6) |
</details>

<details>
<summary>Reproduce the tests</summary>

```bash
uv venv .venv --python 3.12
uv pip install --python .venv/bin/python -r requirements/cpu.txt pytest tblib pytest-asyncio
export VLLM_TARGET_DEVICE=cpu PYTHONPATH=$PWD
# On an arm64 host without Triton, vLLM runs its standalone CPU model runner, which rejects
# speculative decoding at config time: 82 of these tests fail with that error, 79 of them
# main's. Scheduler tests start no model runner, so lift the check, as x86 and GPU hosts have it:
printf 'from vllm.platforms.cpu import CpuPlatform\nCpuPlatform.uses_standalone_cpu_model_runner = classmethod(lambda cls: False)\n' > lift_cpu_runner_check.py
.venv/bin/python -m pytest -q -p lift_cpu_runner_check tests/v1/core/test_scheduler.py \
  tests/v1/core/test_priority_scheduler_random.py \
  tests/v1/core/test_priority_preemption_bug.py \
  tests/v1/core/test_async_scheduler.py \
  tests/v1/core/test_deferred_block_free.py \
  tests/v1/core/test_priority_make_room.py
```

The GPU harness and every run's records are in [Flatshare](https://github.com/StevenWang-CY/flatshare) (`benchmarks/results/`), which serves this change backported to v0.32.0.
</details>

## Details

- **Which requests hold prefill back.** The running requests with fewer than `--priority-prefill-budget-cap-tokens` output tokens, counting a step in flight as one token, since its draft tokens may be rejected. While a running slot is free, also a load in flight, for its first `--priority-prefill-budget-cap-tokens` steps, and a request whose KV load is done, for at most that many steps in which the waiting loop does not admit it. And the highest-priority waiting request that is ready to run, if it fits as #65282 counts the room, for at most that many steps in which the waiting loop does not admit it. Only strictly lower priorities are held back, so at one priority nothing changes.
- **How.** A lower-priority running prefill gets no tokens in the step, and vLLM skips it as any request with none. The first lower-priority waiting request is not admitted, but only after its prefix cache and KV connector lookups, so a KV load it needs starts meanwhile; those behind it start theirs when they reach the head. A request with one token left samples like a decode and is never held. No room is made for a waiting request the cap holds back.
- **Requests that hold KV blocks.** The waiting loop drains them first, so one of a lower priority is skipped rather than waited on. It sits out only while a request of its priority or a lower one runs: while it waits, preemption cannot reach its blocks, and the higher-priority request could otherwise preempt only itself for them.
- **Encoder input.** A prefill midway through an encoder input whose output is cached goes on while a request it is held for needs encoder cache space: the cache frees that output only as the prefill consumes it.
- **KV loads.** With async KV loads from a CPU tier, a turn whose load was done still waited for budget the running loop left over, and agent prefill chunks left none for up to 4 s. So a done load holds prefill back, and a load in flight does for its first steps, since a load's completion is seen only at a step boundary.
- **Bounds.** Without a free running slot, neither a waiting request nor a KV load holds anything back, since neither could be admitted. A request whose first tokens are due stops holding after `--priority-prefill-budget-cap-tokens` steps in a row in which it computes nothing: one that fits but is not admitted, for example while its KV connector lookup is pending; one whose KV load is done but which the waiting loop does not reach, because a request ahead of it fails its allocation; and a running prefill scheduled nothing, such as one at an image longer than the long prefill threshold with `--disable-chunked-mm-input`. What such a request waits for may be what it holds back. Its progress resets the count, and the steps in which a higher priority's hold keeps a waiting request out do not count.
- **Costs and limitations.** Lower-priority prefill makes no progress while higher-priority requests' first tokens are due back to back. On the A100 with 256 requests in flight (48 prompt and 64 output tokens, 10% at priority 0; an earlier revision), both changes take the priority 0 TTFT p99 from 574 to 177 ms and the priority 2 TTFT p99 from 1,086 to 7,971 ms.
- **Related.** Stage 2 of the RFC #62532 proposes holding running prefill back for a finished KV load under FCFS, which this PR does for higher priorities. #65339 reserves step budget for waiting requests with cached KV, and #64927 holds waiting requests back to batch their prefills; neither holds lower-priority prefill back for a request's first tokens.
- **The window.** `--priority-prefill-budget-cap-tokens` should cover the first output the application acts on, such as a voice agent's first sentence: 15 tokens at the median and 39 at most for this agent, which is why 48 tokens did better than 16. Open question: should the default stay at 16?

---

@@ -46,6 +46,18 @@ You can monitor the number of preemption requests through Prometheus metrics exp
 
 In vLLM V1, the default preemption mode is `RECOMPUTE` rather than `SWAP`, as recomputation has lower overhead in the V1 architecture.
 
+### Preemption for Higher-Priority Requests
+
+With `--scheduling-policy priority`, a lower `priority` value is handled first, and a waiting request does not preempt running requests by default: a high-priority request that finds the KV cache full waits until lower-priority requests finish, or until one of them is preempted because a running request cannot grow.
+
+`--max-priority-preemptions-per-step N` lets the highest-priority waiting request preempt up to `N` running requests of a strictly lower priority in a step when the KV cache lacks room for its whole sequence, the prompt and any output so far. It is off by default (`0`) and requires `--scheduling-policy priority`. Requests are preempted in the scheduler's usual order, the lowest priority and then the latest arrival, and only as many as make room: the count credits the request's prefix cache hits and allows for the blocks running requests take until the preempted ones' blocks are freed. If `N` preemptions would not make room, none is made. A preempted request recomputes its KV unless prefix caching or a KV offloading connector keeps it, so a small `N`, such as 2, bounds what one step can cost. In a step that schedules a higher-priority prefill, a lower-priority request that holds no KV blocks, preempted or new, is admitted only if its whole sequence fits beside the blocks in-flight prefills still need; a KV load in flight keeps nothing out, and room is made for it again when it is done, if needed. With the option on, vLLM exports the Prometheus counter `vllm:num_priority_preemptions`, which counts these preemptions; `vllm:num_preemptions` counts them too.
+
+```bash
+vllm serve <model> --scheduling-policy priority --max-priority-preemptions-per-step 2
+```
+
+To also keep lower-priority prefill out of a higher-priority request's first tokens, see [Prefill Hold for Higher-Priority Requests](#prefill-hold-for-higher-priority-requests).
+
 ## Chunked Prefill
 
 Chunked prefill allows vLLM to process large prefills in smaller chunks and batch them together with decode requests. This feature helps improve both throughput and latency by better balancing compute-bound (prefill) and memory-bound (decode) operations.
@@ -79,6 +91,19 @@ llm = LLM(model="meta-llama/Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct", max_num_batched_tokens=16384
 
 See related papers for more details (<https://arxiv.org/pdf/2401.08671> or <https://arxiv.org/pdf/2308.16369>).
 
+### Prefill Hold for Higher-Priority Requests
+
+With `--scheduling-policy priority`, a higher-priority request's first tokens share each step with chunks of lower-priority prefills, which lengthen those steps and so its time to first token (TTFT) and the tokens after it. `--priority-prefill-budget-cap` holds lower-priority prefills, running or waiting, back until the higher-priority request has its first `--priority-prefill-budget-cap-tokens` output tokens (16 by default). It is off by default and requires `--scheduling-policy priority`, and `--priority-prefill-budget-cap-tokens` has no effect without it. Set the token count to cover the first output your application acts on, such as a voice agent's first sentence, which can take a few dozen tokens.
+
+The hold starts in the step in which the request fits (a free running slot and KV cache room for its whole sequence) or, with a running slot free, its KV connector load is done. A request that is not admitted or is scheduled nothing, or a load still in flight, holds prefill back for at most `--priority-prefill-budget-cap-tokens` steps, so none can stall it. Decodes are never held, nor is a request with one token left to compute (a full prefix cache hit), nor a prefill midway through an encoder input while a request it is held for needs encoder cache space, since only that prefill's progress frees the space. A lower-priority request whose KV blocks are already allocated, such as one whose KV load is done, sits out only while a request of the same or a lower priority runs: preemption cannot reclaim a waiting request's blocks, so otherwise the higher-priority request could only preempt itself for them. While higher-priority requests' first tokens are due back to back, lower-priority prefill makes no progress. With the option on, vLLM exports the Prometheus counters `vllm:priority_prefill_held_steps` and `vllm:priority_prefill_held_tokens`: the steps it holds prefill back and the prefill tokens it holds back.
+
+```bash
+vllm serve <model> --scheduling-policy priority \
+    --priority-prefill-budget-cap --priority-prefill-budget-cap-tokens 48
+```
+
+When higher-priority requests also wait for KV cache space, combine it with `--max-priority-preemptions-per-step` (see [Preemption for Higher-Priority Requests](#preemption-for-higher-priority-requests)).
+
 ## Parallelism Strategies
 
 vLLM supports multiple parallelism strategies that can be combined to optimize performance across different hardware configurations.
